A B2B Website Reporting Template for Marketing Leaders

A monthly report that connects website work to buyer behaviour, qualified enquiries and the next decision.

PublishedOctober 27, 2026
Last updatedOctober 27, 2026
AuthorFionn LennonFounder, Legency Media
Share
On this page
Section

A B2B website reporting template should connect the work completed to the outcomes the business can verify. Start with qualified enquiries and the condition of the buying process. Then explain acquisition, search and AI visibility, the changes made, and the decisions needed next.

The template below gives a marketing leader a report that colleagues can read without opening several dashboards. It includes an illustrative month, reusable prompts and the definitions needed to avoid comparing incompatible numbers.

Use the same reporting structure each month. Keep supporting exports and detailed investigation available separately. A consistent report makes missing evidence and changes in performance easier to identify.

What belongs in a monthly B2B website report?

Use six sections: the decision summary, acquisition and lead quality, buyer tasks, search and AI visibility, work completed, and the next priorities. Add a short data note naming the measurement period, definitions and important gaps.

For a team running Webflow, search and conversion as a shared programme, this brings the relevant evidence together. A release count can explain what the team delivered. Lead and research evidence can then show what happened after delivery.

Begin by agreeing three things with sales and leadership:

  • What makes an enquiry relevant enough to accept.
  • Which website tasks the marketing team is responsible for improving.
  • Which decisions this report is expected to support.

Those answers determine the report. A company seeking implementation projects may care about scope-fit enquiries. A self-service software company may need activated trials. Reusing another company’s dashboard without adapting the definitions creates an avoidable reporting problem.

1. Write a decision summary

Open with the outcome, the evidence and the next decision. A useful summary can be read on its own.

Use this prompt:

During [period], [defined outcome] changed from [previous count] to [current count].
The change was concentrated in [source, page, segment or stage].
We completed [relevant work] on [date]. The evidence supports [observed result], with [limitation].
We recommend [specific next action]. It needs [owner or approval] by [date].

Avoid making the completed work the assumed cause of every movement. Note overlapping campaigns, a new referral source or a tracking change before attributing the result.

Here is an illustrative summary:

In September, sales accepted seven website enquiries, compared with five in August. The seven came from the established acquisition sources. A new directory referral added 1,200 visits and one supplier pitch. We clarified implementation scope on the main service page on 9 September. Two buyer sessions found the updated explanation, but its effect on enquiry volume has not been isolated. Next month, we will investigate the form’s mobile error rate and test the recovery path before proposing a layout change.

This is invented data demonstrating the format. It is not a Legency client result.

2. Compare acquisition and lead quality

Show the major sources using one counting method and the same reporting period. Keep submitted enquiries and sales-accepted enquiries visible together.

The distinction matters because a form can receive supplier pitches, recruitment requests, duplicates and poor-fit requirements. A change that increases those submissions needs a different response from one that increases relevant opportunities.

Illustrative source review:

  • Established sources: 1,600 visits, 28 submissions and seven accepted enquiries.
  • New directory referral: 1,200 visits, one submission and no accepted enquiry.
  • Combined: 2,800 visits, 29 submissions and seven accepted enquiries.

Established-source submission rate: 28 / 1,600 = 1.75%. Combined submission rate: 29 / 2,800 = approximately 1.04%. The accepted-enquiry rate for established sources is approximately 0.44%.

If August had 1,500 total visits, all from those established sources, with 24 submissions and five accepted enquiries, September would have more accepted enquiries while the combined submission rate fell from 1.60% to 1.04%. The new source changes the aggregate. A falling headline rate alone cannot establish that the website got worse.

Where exact source attribution is unavailable, show the missing share. Keep “direct or unknown” distinct from records collected before source capture was installed.

Google Analytics documents separate user, session and event acquisition scopes. Select one deliberately for each question. A report of first-user acquisition can legitimately differ from a report of the source associated with a later visit.

3. Report the buying tasks that need attention

Choose a few consequential tasks, such as understanding the service scope, assessing implementation requirements or completing an enquiry. Bring behavioural observations and buyer research together around those tasks.

For each task, record:

  • The page and intended audience.
  • The observed problem or completed task.
  • The source and date of the evidence.
  • What the evidence cannot establish.
  • The next investigation or action.

An example might read:

On the implementation page, two relevant buyers could find the integration list but could not tell who owned data migration. The page currently names supported systems without assigning delivery responsibility. We will add that explanation and repeat the task with new participants.

The number describes those sessions. It does not estimate the percentage of all buyers with the problem.

Keep form-stage counts beside error information where possible. For example, report the number of distinct sessions reaching a form and completing it, then describe any verified error that prevents recovery.

A high exit rate has several possible explanations. Someone may have found an answer, ruled out the offer, encountered friction or opened another tab. Use the observation to choose an investigation. The B2B website performance scorecard provides a reusable evidence record for these findings.

4. Keep search and AI observations distinct

Report organic search clicks, visible search demand and the pages that answer relevant questions. Add AI answer observations as a separately defined measure.

For search, name the query or topic, market where relevant, measured period and destination page. Distinguish a tool’s single ranking check from average position across observed impressions.

For AI answers, document:

  • The question set and why those questions matter.
  • The engines, markets and collection dates.
  • Valid answers checked and missing or failed checks.
  • Brand mentions and citations to the company website.
  • Referral visits observed on the website.
  • Qualified enquiries attributed where evidence exists.

An illustrative panel could contain 20 questions checked on three engines. If 56 of 60 planned checks produce valid answers and 14 cite the site, report 14 of 56 valid answers, or 25%, with four missing checks. Keep that result scoped to the sampled panel. Also show counts per engine and market, so the total cannot conceal missing coverage in one segment.

Do not fold those citations into website traffic. A citation can be seen without a visit, and a visit can arrive without an identifiable referrer. Separate columns preserve what each source actually measured.

Google’s June 2026 announcement describes dedicated generative-AI impression reports, with page and country breakdowns. Its August update confirms worldwide rollout. Use that separate view where relevant; overall Web totals still blend discovery routes. Neither measure identifies a qualified enquiry. Google’s reporting announcement.

5. Connect delivery to an acceptance check

Show what changed on the website and whether the change works. A task marked complete in a project tool is one source of information; the report should also name the verification.

A compact delivery entry can contain:

Change: Added the implementation ownership explanation to the service page.
Released: 9 September.
Verified: Production copy, mobile layout and relevant internal links.
Outcome evidence: New usability sessions scheduled.
Claim supported now: Buyers can access the explanation on the live page.

This keeps a release from being described as a proven conversion improvement before that evidence exists.

For an experiment, add the hypothesis, allocation, eligible sample, primary measure, planned stopping rule and result. State whether the outcome was positive, negative, inconclusive or invalid because of a measurement problem.

Microsoft’s research on sample ratio mismatch explains why assignment and data-quality checks belong before result interpretation. A chart with a positive change is not enough to establish a trustworthy experiment.

The same discipline applies to a performance repair. A faster laboratory result proves an improvement in that test environment. Report any real-user measurements separately and wait for commercial evidence before claiming additional enquiries.

6. End with the decisions for next month

Give every recommendation an owner, a reason and a way to assess completion. Keep the number of priorities within the team’s delivery capacity.

Use these fields:

Decision or action:
Evidence supporting it:
Expected buyer benefit:
What remains uncertain:
Owner and dependencies:
Delivery date:
Acceptance check:
Follow-up measure and date:

The expected benefit is a hypothesis unless the effect is already established. Write it in terms the team can examine, such as helping buyers understand which integrations are included.

For a low-traffic site, the next action may be five carefully recruited buyer sessions, a tracking repair or a technical investigation. Choose the sample and method for the research question. An experiment should enter the plan when its eligible traffic and detectable effect make a useful decision feasible.

Our low-traffic CRO guide explains how to choose among these methods.

Which definitions should stay beside the numbers?

Include a data note that is short enough to survive forwarding. It should answer the questions that could change how someone interprets the result.

Reporting period: start and end dates, timezone, comparison period and whether both periods contain complete days.

Traffic unit: users, sessions, browser-tab visits or page views. If a session can cross midnight, explain whether the selected report deduplicates it across days.

Conversion: the event or business state counted. State whether repeated events in a session are deduplicated.

Qualification: the acceptance rule, review owner and review deadline. For example, sales might classify new enquiries weekly, leaving recent submissions awaiting review.

Attribution: source model, capture coverage and known limitations. Record any date on which measurement began or changed.

Commercial lag: the date at which enquiry cohorts will be reassessed. A form submitted this week may become an opportunity later. Avoid comparing a mature cohort with a new one as if both have had equal time to progress.

A blank measure should carry an explanation. Use “not captured”, “awaiting qualification” or “insufficient sample” when those states describe the evidence. Reserve zero for a measured absence.

How do you keep the report manageable?

Put the decision summary and next actions in the main report. Use a small set of consistent measures, with evidence links for anyone who needs the detail.

Keep two supporting records behind it. The change log records releases and measurement changes. The evidence log records exports, buyer research and experiment results. These records make it possible to investigate a movement without rebuilding the month from memory.

Give one person responsibility for reconciling website submissions with the private enquiry or CRM records. Give another owner responsibility for classifying the business outcome if that sits with sales. The marketing lead can then explain both the number and its status.

Rialto can supply saved site, content, behaviour and AI-answer observations where coverage exists. The report still needs the organisation’s qualification decisions and the limitations of each source. Connecting those records is part of the reporting work.

Frequently asked questions

Should we report conversion rate when enquiry counts are small?

Show the count and denominator alongside the rate, and describe the uncertainty. Two submissions out of 100 sessions produce a 2% observed rate; that arithmetic alone is a weak basis for forecasting. Use several comparable periods and supporting research before making a large investment decision.

How do we report a test that did not find a winner?

State the result and what the test could reliably detect. Preserve the original hypothesis and stopping rule. An inconclusive result may leave an important question open; a negative result can justify keeping the original version. Both belong in the record.

Should the report include competitor conversion benchmarks?

Use a benchmark only when its audience, traffic, conversion definition and measurement method are relevant and disclosed. Many published rates combine unlike businesses. Your own comparable baseline and accepted-enquiry data provide a clearer starting point for an improvement decision.

Can this template be used after a Webflow migration?

Yes. Add launch acceptance checks, search coverage, redirect and form verification, and the date measurement was restored. Compare equivalent periods and annotate campaign changes. Treat the migration’s technical delivery and its later business outcomes as separate questions.
